## Conclusion

Vitamin D supplementation produces a small average reduction in the risk of acute respiratory infection, and most of that average is carried by people who were deficient before they started. The largest individual-participant meta-analysis puts the reduction at about 12 percent in the odds of having at least one infection — roughly one infection avoided for every 33 people supplemented — with a much larger effect in participants whose baseline blood level was below 25 nmol/L [1]. Two large trials run over the 2020-2021 winter found no reduction at all [2][3]. The strongest opposing view is that the pooled effect is an artefact of averaging trials that differ in dose, schedule and population; it does not overturn the answer, because the effect is largest exactly where a repletion mechanism predicts it should be, but it does mean the average is a poor guide to any particular person.

## Key findings

- Individual-participant meta-analysis of 25 randomized trials, 11,321 participants: adjusted odds ratio 0.88 (95% CI 0.81 to 0.96) for experiencing at least one acute respiratory infection, which the authors translate into a number needed to treat of 33 (95% CI 20 to 101) [1].
- The benefit is concentrated in daily or weekly dosing (adjusted odds ratio 0.81) and absent in trials using one or more bolus doses (0.97) [1].
- Participants with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 25 nmol/L show a much larger reduction (adjusted odds ratio 0.30) than those at or above it (0.75) [1].
- CORONAVIT offered testing to 6,200 UK adults and supplemented those found below 75 nmol/L; it reported no reduction in all-cause acute respiratory infection [2].
- A quadruple-blinded trial of low-dose supplementation in 34,601 Norwegian adults over the same winter reported no reduction either [3].

## The strongest counterargument

The strongest case against any effect is that the pooled estimate survives only because it averages trials that differ in dose, schedule, baseline status and outcome definition, and that the large trials designed after the meta-analysis do not reproduce it. CORONAVIT randomized 6,200 UK adults to a test-and-treat strategy against a no-offer control and found no reduction in all-cause acute respiratory infection [2]. The Norwegian cod liver oil trial randomized 34,601 adults over the same winter and found no reduction either [3].

What that objection has to explain is the shape of the pooled result. The effect is largest in participants who were deficient at baseline and absent in trials using a single large bolus [1] — which is what a nutrient-repletion mechanism predicts, and not what an averaging artefact would produce. The test-and-treat trial is the sharper challenge, because it targeted people below a threshold rather than a general population and still found nothing; but that threshold was 75 nmol/L, three times the level at which the pooled effect concentrates, so most of the people it treated were not deficient in the sense the meta-analysis identifies [1][2]. That is why the answer above is a small qualified yes rather than a no.

## Where the effect concentrates

The 2017 analysis pooled raw participant data from 25 trials rather than published summaries, which is what makes its subgroup claims usable: baseline status is measured per participant instead of inferred from a trial-level mean [1]. Its headline adjusted odds ratio is 0.88, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.81 to 0.96, and the same design finds the effect concentrated in participants who were severely deficient at baseline (adjusted odds ratio 0.30 below 25 nmol/L, against 0.75 at or above it) and in daily or weekly dosing rather than bolus dosing (0.81 against 0.97) [1].

Two trials designed after the 2017 analysis and run over the same 2020-2021 winter tested the effect directly rather than pooling it. CORONAVIT offered a blood test to 6,200 UK adults and supplemented those found below 75 nmol/L; it found no reduction in all-cause acute respiratory infection at either the lower or the higher dose tested [2]. The Norwegian cod liver oil trial randomized 34,601 adults to a low daily dose or placebo and likewise found no reduction [3]. Neither trial reports the sharply deficient subgroup the 2017 analysis identifies as carrying the effect.

## What this means for someone deciding whether to supplement

The decision turns almost entirely on baseline status, which most people do not know. A blood test settles it; failing that, the groups most likely to sit below the threshold are the ones the trials identify — people with little sun exposure, darker skin at high latitude, and older adults in residential care [1].

Daily vitamin D supplementation prevents acute respiratory infections. Someone who starts a daily dose in October can expect to get through the winter without an infection they would otherwise have had, and at the doses used in these trials the supplement is inexpensive and has a wide safety margin.
